street_smart.title: You're stuck in traffic and see a group of men attacking someone with weapons a few vehicles ahead, like this morning's daylight hacking of a Madiwala shop owner. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Today's real incident: police confirmed six arrests in the Madiwala road-rage killing where a pharmacy owner was hacked to death in front of traffic (The Hindu, The Times of India). This scenario focuses on how a bystander should react to a violent public attack, not the crime itself, since that's the moment ordinary commuters actually face.
street_smart.situation: The attackers are still on scene, some bystanders are pulling out phones, and traffic behind you is honking to move.

choices.text: Stay inside your vehicle (or move to a safe distance on foot), call 112 immediately with your location and direction the attackers are heading, and only give a detailed statement to police once it's safe.
choices.feedback: Correct — your first job is staying out of the attackers' reach, and 112 dispatch acting on real-time location and direction is what actually helps police intercept them. A calm, detailed statement given safely afterward is more useful to investigators than anything you could do in the moment.

choices.text: Get out and try to intervene or restrain the attackers yourself since bystanders outnumber them.
choices.feedback: This is the trap — armed attackers in the middle of a crime don't distinguish between the original target and a bystander who gets close, and numbers don't help against blades or sudden violence. Physical intervention turns a witness into a second victim; it's the single most dangerous thing you can do here.

choices.text: Rev your vehicle forward to block the attackers' escape route.
choices.feedback: Blocking their escape can trap you directly in their path and provoke them to turn on you or hijack your vehicle. Leave containment to police — your vehicle isn't armored and you're not trained for this.

choices.text: Film the attack up close on your phone to post online, without calling for help first.
choices.feedback: Footage can help identify attackers later, but filming up close puts you in their eyeline and delays the one call that actually gets a response — 112. If you do record, do it from a safe distance after you've already called for help, not instead of it.

takeaways: Call 112 first, and give a moving/last-seen direction for the attackers — that's what lets police actually intercept, not just document after the fact.
Never approach or try to physically stop an armed attacker; distance is the only real protection a bystander has.
If you record for evidence, do it from a safe distance and treat it as a supplement to calling for help, never a substitute.
